title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Summary

Speech acts: utterances that use a particular locution with a conventional meaning to achieve a certain social effect.
Conversational implicatures: inferences tied to particular speech acts, based on:

general principles of rational, cooperative communication (Grice 1975);
conventional meanings.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Where do we go next?

→ conventional meaning



First, we need to develop methods for observing and classifying inference types.
Then, we can focus on the conventional stuff:

study how it is encoded in linguistic expressions.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Defining inference
What is an inference?

A relation between expressions of a language.

\(E_{1} ↝ E_{2}\)

Typically, \(E_{2}\) is a declarative sentence.




Jo did some of the readings.  ↝ Jo didn’t do all of the readings.
Could you bring the dog inside?  ↝ There is a dog.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
This class
Semantics is the study of conventional meaning in natural language.

Goal: give a ridiculously precise account of the inferences that linguistic expressions trigger.
If we can do this, then we have captured what these expressions mean\(_{NN}\).

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
A taxonomy of inference types

Some types of inference observable in natural language:

entailment
conversational implicature
presupposition
conventional implicature

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Entailment

A relationship between declarative sentences.
If \(S_{1}\) entails \(S_{2}\), then whenever \(S_{1}\) is true, \(S_{2}\) must be true.

Jo has at least three siblings.  ↝ Jo has at least two siblings.

Entailments are non-defeasible.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-defeasibility of entailments

#Jo has at least three siblings, {and, but} she doesn’t have at least two siblings.
# Jo is Bo’s sibling, {and, but} Jo and Bo aren’t siblings.
#No one came to class, {and, but} it’s not the case that Julian didn’t come to class.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Conversational implicature

Typically a relationship between utterances of declarative sentences.
If an utterance of \(S_{1}\) conversationally implicates \(S_{2}\), then the utterance means\(_{NN}\) \(S_{2}\).
Conversational implicatures are defeasible.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Defeasibility of conversational implicatures

Jo did some of the readings. In fact, she did all of them.
I want something with lots of caffeine. In fact, I want a matcha latte.
Context: Jo is writing a letter of rec. for Bo for the ling. instructor position.  Jo: Bo is very punctual. He has great handwriting. Last, but not least, he’d be a great ling. instructor!

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Presupposition

A relationship between an expression and a declarative sentence.
If \(E\) presupposes \(S\), then whenever an utterance of \(E\) is felicitous, \(S\) is true.

Jo stopped smoking.  ↝ Jo used to smoke.

Presuppositions are non-defeasible.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-defeasibility of presuppositions

#Jo stopped smoking, {and, but} she didn’t used to smoke.
#Jo loves that it’s raining, {and, but} it’s not raining.
#Bo failed the assignment, {and, but} there isn’t an assignment.
#Bo failed the assignment again, {and, but} he hasn’t failed it before.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Entailment vs. presupposition
First pass:

Presuppositions encode background information, needed to make sense of some expression.

Express what must already be in the common ground (Stalnaker 1978).

Entailments encode information about what is said.

Express information, e.g., which is being added to the common ground.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
The negation test
Second pass:

Presuppositions project, whereas entailments do not.



Jo demonstrated that she’s good at Go. 
Jo loves that she’s good at Go.


Jo didn’t demonstrate that she’s good at Go. 
Jo doesn’t love that she’s good at Go.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
More!

Bo brought the dog to his place of work.


Bo didn’t bring a dog to his place of work. 
Bo didn’t bring the dog to his place of work.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
The question test


Did Jo demonstrate that she’s good at Go?
Does Jo love that she’s good at Go?


Did Jo bring a dog to his place of work? 
Did Jo bring the dog to his place of work?

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
The conditional test


If Jo demonstrated that she’s good at Go, she’ll have to join the Go league. 
If Jo loves that she’s good at Go, she’ll have to join the Go league.


If Bo brought a dog to his place of work, the boss will be mad. 
If Bo brought the dog to his place of work, the boss will be mad.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Families of sentences
These tests are known as family-of-sentence tests (Chierchia and McConnell-Ginet 1990).

Given a sentence \(S_{1}\), from which you can infer \(S_{2}\):

negate \(S_{1}\);
question \(S_{1}\);
put \(S_{1}\) into the antecedent of a conditional.



If \(S_{2}\) survives (i.e., projects), probably a presupposition.

text:
Hey, wait a minute!
The hey, wait a minute test (Fintel 2004).

Bo: You love that you’re good at Go.  Jo: Hey, wait a minute! I’m not good at Go!
Bo: You demonstrated that you’re good at Go!  Jo: #Hey, wait a minute! I’m not good at Go!  Jo: No, I didn’t!

Presuppositions are assumed background information.

If Jo is actually good at Go, she loves that she’s good at Go.

title: Intro. to Semantics

Example from last time

Jo did some of the readings.


Quantity implicature: Jo didn’t do all of the readings.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Reasoning

If (a) following Maxim of Quantity, and (b) believe that Jo did all of the readings, then (c) will say Jo did all of the readings.
Speaker did not say that Jo did all of the readings.
Thus either (a) speaker not following Maxim of Quantity, or (b) not the case that speaker believes Jo did all readings.
Because of Grice’s Cooperative Principle, assume speaker following Maxim of Quantity.
Therefore (by 3 and 4), not the case that the speaker believes that Jo did all of the readings.

But why not: Jo didn’t do only some of the readings?


What we need: some notion of “possible alternative”.

Questions under discussion
Asking a question: add the question onto an ongoing record of questions that need to be answered.


Discourse—at least involving assertions—always has the goal of answering some question (Roberts 2012).

There is always a Question Under Discussion (QUD).

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
An extremely general rule
Grice (1975) proposes the Cooperative Principle:

“Make your conversational contribution, such as is required, at the stage at which is occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange in which you are engaged.”


Basic hypotheses:

Humans are rational agents.
They are cooperative.
Meaning arises from principles of rational cooperation.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Maxims
Grice describe four maxims:

Quality
Quantity
Relation
Manner

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Quality
Part 1: only say that which you believe to be true.

Part 2: only say that which you have enough evidence for.



Who else said something like this?

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Quantity
Part 1: make your contribution as informative as necessary.

Part 2: don’t overdo it.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Relation
Make your contribution relevant.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Manner
Four parts:

Avoid obscurity.
Avoid ambiguity.
Be brief.
Be orderly.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Distinguishing types of act
Austin (1962) classified speech acts at distinct levels.

Locutionary act: an act of uttering a particular expression.

e.g., interrogative vs. imperative vs. declarative

Illocutionary act: an an act of uttering something with a particular intended discourse effect.

e.g., question vs. comamand vs. assertion

Perlocutionary effects: the worldly effects an utterance actually has.

e.g., question answered, command fulfilled, assertion believed

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Illocutionary uptake
An illocutionary act may be successful or unsuccessful.

Successful if it has the intended social consequence (it has uptake).
Unsuccessful if it does not have this consequence (it does not have uptake).

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Uptakes for different acts

the bet is accepted

addressee accepts the obligation to answer

It’s 1:20pm.

addressee accepts (in some sense) the truth of the sentence

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Assertions
Stalnaker (1978) introduces the notion of the common ground.

set of propositions


Uptake of an assertion:

addressee accepts the meaning of the sentence into the common ground.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Force and content
Illocutionary acts can be characterized along at least two dimensions:

illocutionary force: what kind of intended social effect is involved?

assertoric force, imperative force, interrogative force

content: utterance-specific aspects of conveyed meaning

assertions: sets of possible worlds (“truth conditions”)
commands: “satisfaction conditions”
questions: “answerhood conditions”

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Lewis (1975) on language
What are languages?

Lewis: collections of pairs of forms and meanings

Form: sign, sound, mark, etc.
Meaning: set (i.e., collection) of possible states of affairs, things in the world, etc.



What is language?

A human social activity in which people produce certain forms.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Relating them
Lewis introduces a convention to define language use:

“…the convention whereby a population P uses a language ξ is a convention of truthfulness and trust in ξ.”

Truthfulness: try never to utter sentences of ξ that are not true in ξ.
Trust in ξ: impute truthfulness in ξ to others. Believe the things that others tell you.

title: Intro. to Semantics

Communication and meaning
Grice (1957): conceptual analysis of the word ‘mean’.

This rainy weather means we’ll probably be taxiing for a while.
Jo’s gesture means that she wants you to walk over.
“Bo devoured the beans” means that Bo ate the beans aggressively.

“Bo devoured the beans” means that Bo ate the beans aggressively, but in fact, Bo didn’t eat the beans aggressively.

title: Intro. to Semantics

Jo meant by her gesture that she wants you to walk over.

Natural and non-natural meaning

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-natural meaning

Something means\(_{NN}\) that \(p\) if things of its kind tend to produce a belief in an observer that \(p\) is true.

sun being out makes people believe it’s daytime…

text:

title: Intro. to Semantics

An extremely general rule
Grice (1975) proposes the Cooperative Principle:

“Make your conversational contribution, such as is required, at the stage at which is occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange in which you are engaged.”


Basic hypotheses:

Humans are rational agents.
They are cooperative.
Meaning arises from principles of rational cooperation.

Maxims
Grice describe four maxims:

Quality
Quantity
Relation
Manner

title: Intro. to Semantics

Part 1: only say that which you believe to be true.

Part 2: only say that which you have enough evidence for.



Who else said something like this?

Quantity
Part 1: make your contribution as informative as necessary.

Part 2: don’t overdo it.

title: Intro. to Semantics

Relation
Make your contribution relevant.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Manner
Four parts:

Avoid obscurity.
Avoid ambiguity.
Be brief.
Be orderly.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Summary

Speech acts: utterances that use a particular locution with a conventional meaning to achieve a certain social effect.
Conversational implicatures: inferences tied to particular speech acts, based on:

general principles of rational, cooperative communication (Grice 1975);
conventional meanings.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Where do we go next?

→ conventional meaning



First, we need to develop methods for observing and classifying inference types.
Then, we can focus on the conventional stuff:

study how it is encoded in linguistic expressions.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Defining inference
What is an inference?

A relation between expressions of a language.

\(E_{1} ↝ E_{2}\)

Typically, \(E_{2}\) is a declarative sentence.




Jo did some of the readings.  ↝ Jo didn’t do all of the readings.
Could you bring the dog inside?  ↝ There is a dog.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Data collection
Where do inferences come from?

Speakers of the language!

Your friends.
Laboratory experiments.
Large crowd-sourced inference judgment studies.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
This class
Semantics is the study of conventional meaning in natural language.

Goal: give a ridiculously precise account of the inferences that linguistic expressions trigger.
If we can do this, then we have captured what these expressions mean\(_{NN}\).

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
A taxonomy of inference types

Some types of inference observable in natural language:

entailment
conversational implicature
presupposition
conventional implicature

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Entailment

A relationship between declarative sentences.
If \(S_{1}\) entails \(S_{2}\), then whenever \(S_{1}\) is true, \(S_{2}\) must be true.

Jo has at least three siblings.  ↝ Jo has at least two siblings.

Entailments are non-defeasible.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-defeasibility of entailments

#Jo has at least three siblings, {and, but} she doesn’t have at least two siblings.
# Jo is Bo’s sibling, {and, but} Jo and Bo aren’t siblings.
#No one came to class, {and, but} it’s not the case that Julian didn’t come to class.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Conversational implicature

Typically a relationship between utterances of declarative sentences.
If an utterance of \(S_{1}\) conversationally implicates \(S_{2}\), then the utterance means\(_{NN}\) \(S_{2}\).
Conversational implicatures are defeasible.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Defeasibility of conversational implicatures

Jo did some of the readings. In fact, she did all of them.
I want something with lots of caffeine. In fact, I want a matcha latte.
Context: Jo is writing a letter of rec. for Bo for the ling. instructor position.  Jo: Bo is very punctual. He has great handwriting. Last, but not least, he’d be a great ling. instructor!

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Presupposition

A relationship between an expression and a declarative sentence.
If \(E\) presupposes \(S\), then whenever an utterance of \(E\) is felicitous, \(S\) is true.

Jo stopped smoking.  ↝ Jo used to smoke.

Presuppositions are non-defeasible.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-defeasibility of presuppositions

#Jo stopped smoking, {and, but} she didn’t used to smoke.
#Jo loves that it’s raining, {and, but} it’s not raining.
#Bo failed the assignment, {and, but} there isn’t an assignment.
#Bo failed the assignment again, {and, but} he hasn’t failed it before.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Entailment vs. presupposition
First pass:

Presuppositions encode background information, needed to make sense of some expression.

Express what must already be in the common ground (Stalnaker 1978).

Entailments encode information about what is said.

Express information, e.g., which is being added to the common ground.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
The negation test
Second pass:

Presuppositions project, whereas entailments do not.



Jo demonstrated that she’s good at Go. 
Jo loves that she’s good at Go.


Jo didn’t demonstrate that she’s good at Go. 
Jo doesn’t love that she’s good at Go.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:

Bo brought a dog to his place of work. 
Bo brought the dog to his place of work.


Bo didn’t bring a dog to his place of work. 
Bo didn’t bring the dog to his place of work.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
The question test


Did Jo demonstrate that she’s good at Go?
Does Jo love that she’s good at Go?


Did Jo bring a dog to his place of work? 
Did Jo bring the dog to his place of work?

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
The conditional test


If Jo demonstrated that she’s good at Go, she’ll have to join the Go league. 
If Jo loves that she’s good at Go, she’ll have to join the Go league.


If Bo brought a dog to his place of work, the boss will be mad. 
If Bo brought the dog to his place of work, the boss will be mad.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Families of sentences
These tests are known as family-of-sentence tests (Chierchia and McConnell-Ginet 1990).

Given a sentence \(S_{1}\), from which you can infer \(S_{2}\):

negate \(S_{1}\);
question \(S_{1}\);
put \(S_{1}\) into the antecedent of a conditional.



If \(S_{2}\) survives (i.e., projects), probably a presupposition.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Hey, wait a minute!
The hey, wait a minute test (Fintel 2004).

Bo: You love that you’re good at Go.  Jo: Hey, wait a minute! I’m not good at Go!
Bo: You demonstrated that you’re good at Go!  Jo: #Hey, wait a minute! I’m not good at Go!  Jo: No, I didn’t!

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Disappearing presuppositions

If Bo has a dog, he brought the dog to his place of work.
If Jo is actually good at Go, she loves that she’s good at Go.



It’s not true that Bo has a dog and that he brought the dog to his place of work.
It’s not true that Jo is good at Go and that she loves that she’s good at Go.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Changing presuppositions

If Jo has any friends in Gainesville, she loves that she gets to see them.  ↝ If Jo has any friends in Gainesville, she gets to see them.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Conventional implicatures

The class is taught by Julian, who enjoys syntax.  ↝ Julian enjoys syntax.
The class isn’t taught by Julian, who enjoys syntax.  ↝ Julian enjoys syntax.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
